The outage, which began Thursday (November 12) and peaked in the afternoon, affected Microsoft 365 products like Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, leaving many workers and government agencies unable to send or receive emails, attend online meetings, or complete daily tasks. Microsoft updated customers Friday morning, stating it was "continuing to see improvements in service availability," with email queues "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels." However, the company warned that "some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as recovery continues." The outage had widespread effects. Municipal governments in cities such as Baltimore County, Maryland; Jacksonville, Florida; and Austin, Texas, reported being unable to send or receive emails, though emergency services like 911 were not impacted. In Europe, the United Kingdom's government and National Health Service reported disrupted email services, causing some hospitals to advise patients to call by phone instead. Some British courts had to halt proceedings, and police encouraged people to use phone calls for urgent crime reports.

ARLINGTON, Va., Nov. 13, 2026 /CNW/ -- In response to the Microsoft 365 outage that began on November 12, Infotech, a global research and API-driven advisory firm, is recommending that CIOs verify the recovery of business-critical workflows, integrations, and security controls before declaring normal operations restored. The firm's new research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, also advises organizations to document service disruptions and preserve evidence for potential service level agreement claims. The outage began Thursday afternoon with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas and affected functions in Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender. Thursday night, servers that had returned to service failed again under load, and Microsoft added capacity and began rolling back a recent network change. According to the note's midday ET update on November 13, availability was improving, but intermittent issues persisted, and Microsoft had not given a restoration time. At that point, Microsoft had reported no evidence of malicious activity, and the root cause was still under investigation.

Microsoft outage highlights risks of relying on a single technology provider

A global Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services, affecting businesses, government agencies, healthcare services and law enforcement across several countries. The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour. Story continues below this ad The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents. Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer. As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday. By Friday morning in the U.S., Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Still, it warned of potential intermittent access and ongoing delays. On Thursday, the company said it had “successfully restored” Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.
